newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A -- Deflation, price measures Part IV.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A -- Deflation, price measures Part IV.

text.p: Following are excerpts from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's question-and-answer session with the Senate Banking Committee after the second day of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.
Sen. Mack (R-Florida): "... Are we moving from a time of disinflation to deflation and what are the risks inherent?"

Greenspan: "I would say that while it is certainly the case that the measured inflation rate has come down, and indeed if you adjust, take the bias out of the data, then the inflation rate is down still more, there are none of the characteristics in this economic structure which leads us to conclude that we're moving in a direction of deflation. Deflation clearly is something we should avoid as well. But I see no evidence in the internal structure of what is happening that raises those questions.

"You have to be a little careful about the problem of price measurement. An increasing part of the prices that we're currently publishing are reflecting the very marked declines in prices in an increasing high-tech area.

"Measuring what prices really mean, for a personal computer for example, or for some significant advance in a microchip, is a very interesting technical exercise. We generally tend to measure the units of output in terms of the power of calculation.

"And as you know, the technology is rising and is advancing at such a pace that that power is moving up exponentially. And what that means is that since market revenue...divided by production is what we mean by price, we are getting very dramatic declines in price. Even though the price of a PC has not changed much over the years, the power that is put into it has made the implicit price correctly measured by the value of the power go down dramatically.

"The reason I raise this question is that it's not clear to me that everyone uses all of that power, and that when one is trying to ask 'what is the real price change of a particular piece of equipment,' it's not self-evident to me that everyone would agree that the value increases that they see that are implicit in the prices that we publish, reflect the improvements that they're able to get out of the machine.

"The bottom line of all of this is that some of the ways in which we measure price are increasingly complex, and have ranges of error in them. And the more we shift towards the increased technology types of equipment, the greater the pressure for prices to decline in a measured form. And this is the reason why we've had previous discussions about this and the various indexing of programs, of federal programs and getting judgments about what the biases are.

"There's another issue which we've always discussed, mainly the increasing difficulty of measuring what we mean by price. So I want to be careful here that when we talk about deflation ... careful about not assuming that because we are shifting towards the type of equipment which prices are falling, that therefore we have what we call financial deflation. That is a different type of concept, something we don't fully understand."
Mack: "What would be the indicators you look at that would signal to you that we may be moving into a time of deflation?"

Greenspan: "I would say that I would be more concerned about deflation as it really reflects asset values as well as prices. In other words, the whole process of what historically we have looked at as deflation has been characterized not only by product prices falling, but by asset prices falling. ... A much different type of environment in a period of stable asset prices does not create the types of disruptions which are enimical to economic growth. We've seen innumerable cases in our history in which prices have actually been falling, asset prices in fact rising, economic growth looking quite impressive. It is more important to think in terms not of deflation as price deflation per se but as a process which is inimical to economic growth."
